- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 1–3% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >5% from prior day), model should not overreact — cap forecast slope to avoid overshoot; reduce rate of increase by 10–20%.
- If official event net supply is negative and sentiment is bearish, model should not ignore the bearish signal — reduce forecast mean by 2–5% to reflect policy/supply pressure.
- When sentiment swings from bullish to bearish within 3–5 days, model should adjust downward with a lag of 1–2 days to avoid overfitting to recent sentiment.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows mean reversion after a spike, model should reduce forecast slope after day 10–15 to reflect diminishing momentum.
- If official events are frequent and supply net is negative, model should not assume price will continue rising — add a downward bias of 1–3% per 5 events to reflect supply constraints.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.00–0.33), model should not over-forecast — use historical mean or slightly below to avoid false optimism.
- If true outcome deviates from forecast by >5% in first 5 days, adjust forecast slope downward for next 5 days to reflect lagged market reaction.
